news.headline: NCP's Praful Patel meets Sharad Pawar at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai to inquire about health
news.story_lead: NCP's Praful Patel meets Sharad Pawar at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai to inquire about health The 85-year-old Pawar is undergoing treatment at the south Mumbai hospital for a chest and respiratory infection. The hospital said his condition was stable. Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) working president Praful Patel met NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar at Breach Candy Hospital on Thursday to enquire about his health.
news.full_article_text: NCP's Praful Patel meets Sharad Pawar at Breach Candy Hospital in Mumbai to inquire about health The 85-year-old Pawar is undergoing treatment at the south Mumbai hospital for a chest and respiratory infection. The hospital said his condition was stable. Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) working president Praful Patel met NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar at Breach Candy Hospital on Thursday to enquire about his health. Also Read | PM Modi calls Sharad Pawar, advises rest as NCP (SP) chief discharged from hospital The meeting came days after a group of senior NCP leaders, including Patel, met Union home minister Amit Shah in Delhi, triggering speculation about turmoil within the regional party. The NCP, however, denied any internal rift. People aware of the matter said Pawar enquired about what transpired at the meeting with Shah, but Patel told media that no political discussions had taken place. Also Read | Sharad Pawar hospitalised, cuts short drought-hit areas tour “I keep meeting Pawar Saheb and Supriya Sule on and off as we share family ties. We did not discuss politics, as a hospital is not a place for it,” Patel told reporters at the hospital. He added: “Saheb, in his own style, laughingly asked what is going on in politics.” Also Read | Sharad Pawar hospitalised in Mumbai hours after discharge in Pune The Sharad Pawar-founded NCP split in 2023 after a group of party leaders, including Patel, joined the ruling Mahayuti alliance in Maharashtra under the leadership of late Ajit Pawar. Subsequently, the Ajit Pawar faction got the party name and its symbol, while Sharad Pawar's group became NCP (SP). - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Faisal Malik Faisal Malik is a senior journalist with over two and a half decades of experience covering Maharashtra’s politics, governance and public policy with a deep understanding of the state’s political landscape. He is a Senior Assistant Editor at Hindustan Times and has been associated with its Mumbai edition for more than a decade. Based in Mumbai, Faisal currently covers three major political parties in Maharashtra — Congress, Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) and NCP (Sharad Pawar). Over the years, he has extensively reported on major political developments, combining investigative insights with in-depth field reporting. His coverage has spanned a wide range of issues, from drought, farmer suicides, major development projects and grassroots challenges to major electoral battles, including three Lok Sabha and Maharashtra Assembly elections — 2014, 2019 and 2024. Before joining Hindustan Times, he worked with ‘The Asian Age’ and ‘Dainik Bhaskar’. An avid tea enthusiast, he enjoys reading history, Urdu literature and classical poetry. When away from the newsroom, he writes Urdu poetry inspired by human emotions, life's experiences, meaningful reflections and relationships. An amateur photographer, Faisal is passionate about capturing moments that often go unnoticed by the naked eye. Read More

news.full_article_text: Flood relief row: IAS officer files complaint against Odisha BJP MLA, seeks police protection Responding to the allegations, MLA Saroj Padhi claimed that the differences between him and IAS officer Samir Jena had been resolved through mutual discussions. A 2022-batch IAS officer has lodged a police complaint against MLA of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Saroj Kumar Padhi, accusing him of abusing, threatening and intimidating him during a dispute over flood relief distribution in Odisha's Ganjam district on Thursday, and has sought police protection. Samir Kumar Jena, posted as the Chief Development Officer (CDO) and Executive Officer of the Ganjam Zilla Parishad, lodged the complaint with the inspector-in-charge of Aska police station following an alleged altercation with the Aska legislator at the Aska Notified Area Council (NAC) office on November 3. Responding to the allegations, Padhi claimed that the differences between him and Jena had been resolved through mutual discussions. Describing the episode as a misunderstanding, he said the matter had been settled amicably. The allegations According to the complaint, the incident occurred around 7 pm, when Samir Kumar Jena was discussing official matters with the NAC chairperson in the NAC Executive Officer's chamber. BJP MLA Saroj Padhi allegedly entered the room and picked an argument over the distribution of relief materials. When Jena informed him that the relief materials had been distributed as per the instructions of steel and mines minister Bibhuti Bhushan Jena, the MLA allegedly abused him and threatened to kill him, the officer claimed. "The MLA shouted at me and said, ‘What minister are you talking about? I am the minister in Aska. Nothing happens here without my consent. Since last 4-5 days, I am watching your drama. What do you think of yourself? ’," the officer wrote in his FIR. Jena has also alleged that the incident was captured on the office's CCTV cameras. He has sought stringent legal action against the legislator and police protection, stating that the incident had caused him mental distress. The complaint comes amid growing resentment among government officials in Ganjam over the alleged mistreatment of the senior officer, who had been engaged in relief, restoration and rehabilitation work during Cyclone Arnab and the subsequent floods. Officer backed Officials belonging to the Odisha Administrative Service (OAS) and other government cadres rallied behind Jena on Thursday, condemning the alleged incident. A delegation of officers and employees from various departments of the Ganjam Zilla Parishad met the district collector and submitted a memorandum demanding stringent action against the MLA. They also sought adequate security for government personnel engaged in disaster response and relief operations, saying officials should be able to discharge their duties without intimidation. The district collector said government officials must remain committed to their responsibilities in difficult circumstances and that the matter would be brought to the state government's attention. Political turn The controversy took a political turn on Wednesday when a delegation of the opposition Biju Janata Dal (BJD), led by Ganjam district youth wing president Nachiketa Swain, lodged a written complaint against the MLA at Aska police station. State Fisheries and Animal Resources Development Minister Gokulananda Mallik termed the incident unfortunate and said the Aska MLA was remorseful. He expressed confidence that the matter would be resolved amicably, adding that Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi was monitoring the situation. Meanwhile, the Executive Officer of Aska NAC was transferred from Aska to Bhubaneswar on Wednesday, a day after the alleged altercation. The incident has triggered a wider debate in Odisha over the alleged intimidation of government officials engaged in emergency relief and rehabilitation operations in the aftermath of the devastating floods in Ganjam district. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Debabrata Mohanty Debabrata Mohanty is a senior assistant editor of Hindustan Times who works as state correspondent from Odisha covering the state's politics, governance, public policy, natural disasters, environment and its society for close to three decades. With his long years of reporting from the state capital of Bhubaneswar, Mohanty has been known as one of the most experienced and credible journalists covering Odisha for the national English dailies. His reporting combines on-ground detail with deep institutional knowledge detailing the state's changing politics, governance issues, administrative reforms and the functioning of its public institutions. He has regularly reported on issues ranging from legislative developments and public policy implementation. Politics is his core areas of expertise as he closely tracks Odisha's political landscape, including the rise and transformation of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the Biju Janata Dal (BJD), the two principal political parties in Odisha. His long association with the state's political establishment enables him to write on contemporary developments in a larger political context. Mohanty takes a deep interest in writing human interest stories, environmental issues and documenting the impact of cyclones, floods, heatwaves, and other climate-related events in one of the most disaster-prone states. His coverage extends to public health, governance reforms and stories on accountability of government institutions. Before joining Hindustan Times, Mohanty worked with The Indian Express, Mail Today, and The Telegraph, where he covered at least six general elections and as many assembly elections. In 2007, he was selected for the prestigious Chevening Young Indian Print Journalist Programme at the University of Lincoln, United Kingdom, where he received advanced training in print journalism. In 2009 he won the Press Institute of India-International Committee of Red Cross award on conflict reporting for his on-ground reportage of 2008 Kandhamal riots. Read More

news.full_article_text: From rank-based admissions to lower fees: Decoding NMC's proposed NEET-PG reforms The proposed changes also include greater digitisation of counselling, lower fees for non-clinical courses, and a review of residents’ stipends, among others. Postgraduate medical admissions in India could undergo a significant overhaul starting with the 2027 counselling cycle, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) proposing to replace the existing percentile-based qualifying system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS with a rank-only system. The proposed changes also include greater digitisation of counselling, lower fees for non-clinical courses, a review of residents’ stipends and biometric verification to prevent candidates from blocking seats. The proposals are part of the recommendations of a 12-member expert committee constituted by the Union health ministry on July 23, following the Supreme Court’s intervention in a case challenging the sharp reduction in NEET-PG qualifying cut-offs. The Centre has submitted the committee’s report containing findings and recommendations to the court in an affidavit on Tuesday. The reforms aim to address two recurring concerns: vacant postgraduate medical seats and delays in counselling that affect the start of the academic session. However, the rank-only proposal is yet to be incorporated into final regulations and formally notified. Here is what could change and how it would differ from the current system. No more percentile-based qualifying cut-offs? Under the existing system, candidates must secure a prescribed minimum percentile to become eligible for postgraduate medical counselling. A percentile indicates a candidate’s relative performance compared with other test-takers. The authorities can lower the qualifying percentile when seats remain vacant, thereby expanding the pool of candidates eligible for admission. This was at the centre of the controversy following the NEET-PG 2025 counselling process. On January 13, 2026, the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) reduced the qualifying percentile for reserved-category candidates to zero, making candidates scoring as low as minus 40 out of 800 eligible for admission. For general and Economically Weaker Section candidates, the cut-off was reduced from the 50th percentile to the seventh percentile. The decision followed around 9,000 postgraduate seats remaining vacant after the second round of counselling. It was challenged in the Supreme Court by social worker Harisharan Devgan and doctors, who argued that allowing candidates with zero or negative scores to qualify could dilute minimum standards in medical education. What is proposed: Instead of declaring qualifying percentiles and lowering them to make more candidates eligible, candidates would be ranked according to their performance, with counselling conducted based on these ranks. The affidavit states: “NMC is in the process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised, wherein only a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS counselling will be adopted; no percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates.” NMC secretary Dr Raghav Langer communicated the decision to the Director General of Health Services (DGHS) on October 1, according to the affidavit. A senior NMC official told HT that the proposal had been approved in principle, but “the commission would wait for the court’s final directions before proceeding with the next steps, including seeking stakeholders’ suggestions.” The panel has also cautioned that the change should not compromise minimum standards. “The sanctity of NEET examinations should be maintained, and minimum qualifying standards in postgraduate medical education are not diluted to the extent of permitting candidates with grossly inadequate or negative performance to become eligible for admission,” the affidavit said. Counselling to become more digital The committee found that counselling delays were partly linked to manual processes and to gaps in coordination among the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC), the NMC, colleges, and state authorities. Two preliminary MCC audit meetings, held on May 20 and June 3, flagged the reliance on colleges for manual verification of seat matrices, delays in adding newly approved seats and repeated extensions of counselling timelines. Until 2025, MCC depended on colleges to provide and verify seat details. The process was complicated by the fact that newly approved seats could be added by NMC after the first round had begun, requiring further verification and changes to the counselling schedule. Candidates also had to physically visit colleges to complete admission formalities, submit original documents and seek their return when upgrading to another seat. The committee flagged delays and inconvenience linked to document release and fee refunds. What is proposed: The panel has recommended that NMC share an updated and verified seat matrix with MCC well before counselling begins. It has also proposed online sharing of NEET-UG, NEET-PG, MDS and super-speciality examination results with state counselling authorities. A feasibility study for sharing results online with state authorities is under way for the 2027 academic year. The committee has called for counselling to be digitised with minimal human intervention and for MCC to develop standard operating procedures and a project charter that define the responsibilities of different stakeholders. The charter would also record changes ordered by courts or competent authorities as “institutional memory”, the report said. MCC has been asked to prepare summary reports after each counselling exercise and hold stakeholder meetings before and after counselling. What has already changed: Some processes have been introduced in the 2026-27 counselling cycle. These include online release of candidates who upgrade their seats, allowing candidates to accept upgraded seats without first physically returning to their earlier colleges, and changes to fee- and document-related procedures. The report also records the introduction of a query-resolution mechanism, informational videos and an online dashboard. Lower fees for non-clinical courses The committee has flagged vacancies in pre-clinical and para-clinical postgraduate disciplines, which generally attract fewer candidates than clinical specialities such as general medicine, surgery and paediatrics. It has recommended that state fee fixation committees consider charging lower fees for non-clinical courses to encourage candidates to take up these seats. “The fee of non-clinical branches may be a little less so that the candidates feel encouraged to accept the seat and this wastage of medical seats may be prevented,” the report said. The panel has also suggested considering exemptions from compulsory service bonds for candidates admitted to pre-clinical and para-clinical subjects, leaving the decision to state governments. Postgraduate medical admissions in India could undergo a significant overhaul starting with the 2027 counselling cycle, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) proposing to replace the existing percentile-based qualifying system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS with a rank-only system.

The proposed changes also include greater digitisation of counselling, lower fees for non-clinical courses, a review of residents’ stipends and biometric verification to prevent candidates from blocking seats.

The proposals are part of the recommendations of a 12-member expert committee constituted by the Union health ministry on July 23, following the Supreme Court’s intervention in a case challenging the sharp reduction in NEET-PG qualifying cut-offs. The Centre has submitted the committee’s report containing findings and recommendations to the court in an affidavit on Tuesday.

The reforms aim to address two recurring concerns: vacant postgraduate medical seats and delays in counselling that affect the start of the academic session. However, the rank-only proposal is yet to be incorporated into final regulations and formally notified.

news.full_article_text: March 11 OBC creamy layer quota order would not apply retrospectively: Supreme Court The government said the judgment’s operation to all past appointments and admissions would lead to complete chaos The Supreme Court on Friday clarified that its March 11 judgment, which said Other Backward Classes (OBC) candidates cannot be excluded from reservation benefits solely based on their parents’ salary income, will not apply to past appointments after the government opposed the retrospective operation. It said that the judgment was passed in favour of the parties who approached it. Regarding retrospective operation, a bench of Justices PS Narasimha and R Mahadevan said the decided ratio will not lead to reopening of appointments already made. The court said the government is at liberty to have its own policy. It held that its judgment will govern service allocation under the 2025 civil services examination, since the process was ongoing when the judgment was pronounced. The government filed an application in August, saying that the judgment’s operation to all past appointments and admissions would lead to complete administrative chaos. It requested two years to work out equivalent posts similar to Group A and B officers in the government for identifying the creamy layer among those employed in public sector undertakings (PSUs) and private employment. The March 11 judgment gave the government six months to implement it. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta and additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati argued that the application does not question the judgment. “The Union government is only praying for a limited deferral of the operationalisation of the law laid down by this court for a period of two years so that the competing rights can be adjusted consistent with the administrative contingencies and an effective equivalence exercise is carried out,” Bhati argued. “The application of the present judgment to past and ongoing recruitments will gravely prejudice the competing rights of persons who were not even a party to the present litigation and will result in reopening of seniority, cadre allocation of appointees and candidates and result in complete administrative chaos.” Bhati pointed out that the civil service exam recruitment rules for the past year and this year have been issued. She added that some candidates are citing this judgment to seek enhanced allocation opportunities based on the benefits under the March 11 judgment. She said some candidates whose parents are earning even over ₹ 1 crore annually would benefit and be considered as OBC non-creamy layer category by virtue of the implementation of the judgment. The court passed judgment in March on the Union government’s appeals against Madras high court orders. The high court permitted an OBC candidate to be treated as a non-creamy layer candidate, which furthered his career prospects. The candidate recommended for the Indian Police Service under the OBC reservation became entitled to allocation under the Indian Foreign Service. The Supreme Court approved the high court order. It discarded the Union government’s objection that his father worked with a multinational, had a high income, and would come under the creamy layer. It said another candidate was entitled to OBC reservation in the civil services after he was initially refused it because of his father’s PSU employment, which fetched a higher income. Both candidates argued that their parents were excluded on income criteria. They said creamy layer classification was based on posts, and Group A or B, C or D officers were excluded as creamy layer. They argued that similar “equalisation” based on posts should apply to OBC parents working in PSUs and private employment. The March judgment said treating the children of those employed in PSUs or private employment as being excluded from the benefit of reservation only based on their salary income, and without reference to their posts (whether Group A or B, or Group C or D), would lead to hostile discrimination between parties similarly placed. It added that this would amount to equals being treated unequally. The creamy layer notification was issued in 1993 following the landmark Indra Sawhney judgment of 1992. The 1992 judgment allowed 27% reservation for OBCs, subject to exclusion of the creamy layer. The 1993 order identified five occupational categories as the creamy layer. A sixth category was based on an income and wealth test. In 2004, the government issued a clarificatory order. It explained that income from salaries and from other sources (excluding salaries and agricultural land) are to be assessed separately. The 2004 order said exclusion would follow only if either component exceeds the prescribed limit for three consecutive years. The March judgment held that the evolution of the non-creamy layer principle demonstrates that both the 1993 office memorandum and 2004 letter preserve the primacy of status- based exclusion. It said they confine economic exclusion to those falling under the sixth category. “Salary income cannot be mechanically aggregated in a manner that defeats the constitutional objective articulated in Indra Sawhney,” the court said.

Seventy-five per cent of the first Agniveer batch were set to be released under the Agnipath scheme before the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial four-year service an option to remain in service for two more years. news.full_article_text: CAPFs debated merit, ex-Agniveer postings before Union Cabinet’s Agnipath overhaul approval The Cabinet approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial service an option to remain in service The central armed police forces (CAPFs) debated how to assess Agniveer merit for induction and where to post these highly trained soldiers to ensure smooth integration with existing personnel without friction, before all of the short-term military recruits were given a retention option. Seventy-five per cent of the first Agniveer batch were set to be released under the Agnipath scheme before the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial four-year service an option to remain in service for two more years. Agniveers were offered a route to enrol as regular soldiers at the end of the extended period. In March 2023, the government announced a 10% Agniveer quota in CAPFs and exemption from the Physical Efficiency Test when the scheme was first notified. They had to take the written test, and ex-Agniveers could join as constables (general duty), the junior-most functional rank. “The quota increased from 10 to 50% in CAPFs, a substantial increase. More than that, the issue concerned 50% of former soldiers being inducted directly while the other 50% had to clear all tests. It was a challenge to ensure this would not affect the morale of those who had to clear all tests to get inducted,” said an officer. Deep Dive The CAPFs were awaiting clarity on how merit was to be established for the 50% ex-Agniveers because there was to be no test, written or physical, during their induction until the Union Cabinet’s retention approval. Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, who on Wednesday announced the Cabinet’s decision, said there would be no reservation for ex-Agniveers. “The reservation in the paramilitary forces and states was announced when 75% of soldiers were to be released back into society.” He said the defence forces are offering all 75% Agniveers a chance to join back and also enrol as regular soldiers after completing their tenure. “This is why, after this, no reservation, whether in paramilitary forces or state government, will exist because the Indian defence forces are providing them all an opportunity to rejoin for a second engagement period of two years and after that to become regular soldiers in the armed forces.” Merit assessment and integration within CAPFs gained urgency after the government made changes to the Agnipath scheme over the last year. The first two Agniveer batches from the Navy and Air Force were due to complete their tenure in November and December, making them eligible for reemployment in the CAPFs. People aware of the matter said Union home ministry officials held meetings on how to decide merit among the Agniveers and avoid friction between regular CAPF personnel, who have to pass three tests. In November 2025, the government exempted ex-Agniveers from all written, physical efficiency, or physical standard tests for enrolment in the CAPFs. Officials said the ministry also formed an ex-Agniveer cell this year. The cell was taking feedback and inputs from all CAPFs regarding the induction and career progression of the ex-Agniveers. The Central Reserve Police Force was appointed the nodal agency for their induction and career progression across all CAPFs. A second officer said all CAPF chiefs were holding internal discussions with their senior officers on ways to induct the former soldiers into the force in the weeks leading up to Wednesday’s announcement. “This looked like an easy transition, but it is a challenging one. Soldiers are highly trained and motivated.” The second officer said the Agniveer job is proactive, while it is reactive in CAPFs, barring counter-insurgency or counter-militancy operations. “All chiefs were taking inputs to find the best place to post highly trained soldiers and reorient them. ...this would not have been the first time such a transition happened. There are hundreds and thousands of cases, especially in the early years of BSF [Border Security Force] when the force took army personnel on deputation.” The officer added that many officers enjoyed the work culture and decided to continue their service in the CAPFs. “There are also many cases of army officers joining state police forces too.” Brigadier (Retd) Rohit Nautiyal joined the CRPF as a deputy inspector general and was posted in Srinagar in 2022 after serving the Army for 32 years. He retired from the CRPF last week after a three-year tenure post-reemployment. Seventy-five per cent of the first Agniveer batch were set to be released under the Agnipath scheme before the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved giving those failing to make the cut after the initial four-year service an option to remain in service for two more years. Agniveers were offered a route to enrol as regular soldiers at the end of the extended period. In March 2023, the government announced a 10% Agniveer quota in CAPFs and exemption from the Physical Efficiency Test when the scheme was first notified. They had to take the written test, and ex-Agniveers could join as constables (general duty), the junior-most functional rank. “The quota increased from 10 to 50% in CAPFs, a substantial increase. More than that, the issue concerned 50% of former soldiers being inducted directly while the other 50% had to clear all tests. It was a challenge to ensure this would not affect the morale of those who had to clear all tests to get inducted,” said an officer. Deep Dive The CAPFs were awaiting clarity on how merit was to be established for the 50% ex-Agniveers because there was to be no test, written or physical, during their induction until the Union Cabinet’s retention approval. Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, who on Wednesday announced the Cabinet’s decision, said there would be no reservation for ex-Agniveers. “The reservation in the paramilitary forces and states was announced when 75% of soldiers were to be released back into society.” He said the defence forces are offering all 75% Agniveers a chance to join back and also enrol as regular soldiers after completing their tenure. “This is why, after this, no reservation, whether in paramilitary forces or state government, will exist because the Indian defence forces are providing them all an opportunity to rejoin for a second engagement period of two years and after that to become regular soldiers in the armed forces.” Merit assessment and integration within CAPFs gained urgency after the government made changes to the Agnipath scheme over the last year. The first two Agniveer batches from the Navy and Air Force were due to complete their tenure in November and December, making them eligible for reemployment in the CAPFs. People aware of the matter said Union home ministry officials held meetings on how to decide merit among the Agniveers and avoid friction between regular CAPF personnel, who have to pass three tests. In November 2025, the government exempted ex-Agniveers from all written, physical efficiency, or physical standard tests for enrolment in the CAPFs. Officials said the ministry also formed an ex-Agniveer cell this year. The cell was taking feedback and inputs from all CAPFs regarding the induction and career progression of the ex-Agniveers. The Central Reserve Police Force was appointed the nodal agency for their induction and career progression across all CAPFs. A second officer said all CAPF chiefs were holding internal discussions with their senior officers on ways to induct the former soldiers into the force in the weeks leading up to Wednesday’s announcement. “This looked like an easy transition, but it is a challenging one. Soldiers are highly trained and motivated.” The second officer said the Agniveer job is proactive, while it is reactive in CAPFs, barring counter-insurgency or counter-militancy operations. “All chiefs were taking inputs to find the best place to post highly trained soldiers and reorient them. ...this would not have been the first time such a transition happened. There are hundreds and thousands of cases, especially in the early years of BSF [Border Security Force] when the force took army personnel on deputation.” The officer added that many officers enjoyed the work culture and decided to continue their service in the CAPFs. “There are also many cases of army officers joining state police forces too.” Brigadier (Retd) Rohit Nautiyal joined the CRPF as a deputy inspector general and was posted in Srinagar in 2022 after serving the Army for 32 years. He retired from the CRPF last week after a three-year tenure post-reemployment. news.full_article_text: Supreme Court refuses to entertain Azam Khan's bail plea in ED case, urges HC to hear matter Khan was arrested on October 31 in the money laundering case, shortly after he and his son were released from Rampur prison in an alleged dual PAN card case. The Supreme Court on Thursday refused to entertain Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Azam Khan’s plea challenging his arrest in a fresh money laundering case filed by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and urged the Allahabad high court to hear the matter on November 16. “The high court has been granting you liberty at every stage. We do not want to bypass the high court,” a bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi said. Khan was arrested on October 31 in the money laundering case, shortly after he and his son Abdullah Azam Khan were released from Rampur prison in Uttar Pradesh in an alleged dual PAN card case. The latest case pertains to alleged misuse of government funds in the construction of the Mohammad Ali Jauhar University that was established in Rampur by Khan. The 78-year-old SP veteran was produced before the special Ghaziabad court and subsequently sent to judicial custody for 14 days. The top court bench directed the transfer of Khan’s bail petition to the Allahabad high court within two days. It also directed the registrar general of the high court to immediately place the matter before the chief justice, to constitute a division bench for the hearing on November 16. “The division bench is requested to pass order on the prayer for interim relief (bail),” it said. Appearing for Khan, senior advocate Kapil Sibal alleged that ED has opened 28 new Enforcement Case Information Reports (ECIR) based on predicate offences dating back to 2006. He argued that the whole purpose of arresting his client now is to keep him in custody ahead of the assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh early next year. “Your argument may have substance but if we say something in your favour it will prejudice the case. We will request the high court to decide on the very first day of reopening after the Diwali vacation. If there is a vacation bench, we will ask the chief justice to consider,” the bench said. Sibal said the Allahabad high court granted Khan bail on October 29 in the dual PAN card case, but ED officials were already waiting outside the jail before he could walk out. He cited Khan's age and the 87 previous cases in which he has secured bail. He also pointed out that the latest arrest comes ahead of the state assembly elections scheduled to be held next year. “They have shown goats and cows as proceeds of crime, does it not shock judicial conscience? And 28 fresh cases have been lodged by ED. It will take years for me to be released in all these matters. This is pure persecution as they want me to die in jail. They knew I would be released by the high court, so they filed a fresh ECIR. This is to make sure in the next elections I am not there,” he said. The bench told Sibal: “It appears the nub of the ED material is Income Tax proceedings where a substantial amount has been shown as part of the management of the university. Your argument is that it is malafide. There is a substantial passage of time but what the ED plead is that because of your supervening influence, FIR was not registered back then.” It was referring to the SP rule in Uttar Pradesh in 2006, when party leader Mulayam Singh Yadav was chief minister. The court also said one of the ECIRs is with regard to misuse of Haj Committee funds. On October 29, Khan was granted bail in the dual PAN case, in which he was awarded a 10-year prison term. The high court suspended the sentence but refused to stay the conviction.

news.full_article_text: Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam move Supreme Court for bail in 2020 Delhi riots case Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam have approached the Supreme Court for bail, saying protected witnesses are unlikely to be examined before January 5, 2027. Former Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) scholar Umar Khalid and student activist Sharjeel Imam, accused in the larger conspiracy case linked to the 2020 Delhi riots, have moved the Supreme Court seeking bail, arguing that the one-year embargo imposed by the court on January 5 is nearing its end even as the examination of protected witnesses is unlikely to be completed by then. The petitions filed on Wednesday rely on the court’s observations denying them bail in the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case while giving them liberty to revive their bail pleas after the examination of protected witnesses or the expiry of one year, whichever is earlier. The court had held that the role attributed to the duo stood on a “qualitatively different footing” as it enlarged five accused persons on bail in the riots case while segregating the case of Khalid and Imam. The court had said, “We are of the opinion that on the completion of the examination of the protected witnesses relied upon by the prosecution, or upon the expiry of a period of one year from the date of this order, whichever is earlier, these two appellants would be at liberty to renew their prayer for grant of bail before the jurisdictional court.” Both had later approached the Delhi high court, which turned down their bail pleas on September 30, citing the one-year embargo fixed by the top court. The high court bench of justices Pratibha M Singh and Dinesh Bhatt said it was not possible for it to modify the Supreme Court’s order. Challenging this dismissal, the two have urged the top court to consider the present position as they remain incarcerated for six years and the prosecution has failed to examine even one of the more than 900 witnesses named in the case. According to the prosecution, there are 47 protected witnesses. Khalid has filed his plea through advocate N Sai Vinod, while Imam has approached the top court through advocate Fauzia Shakil. The two accused in the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case informed the top court that the case is at the stage of arguments on charge. They claimed that arguments on the framing of charges concluded on July 13, but the trial has not proceeded as the trial judge has decided to await the outcome of a Supreme Court judgment on a co-accused’s plea to inspect unrelied documents. The judgment was reserved by the top court in this case on September 1. The petitioners have argued that “on no fair assessment can examination of protected witnesses be expected to commence, much less to conclude, before January 5, 2027 or for a considerable period thereafter.” In such a scenario, they stated that “continued detention is no longer process-oriented and becomes punitive by reason of unreasonable and unjustified delay.” Following the January 5 order, the accused pointed out a further development — another coordinate bench of the Supreme Court, on May 18, in an unrelated case relating to bail under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), found fault with the January 5 decision and held that a delay in trial should entitle an accused person booked under the UAPA to bail. The January 5 decision was given by a bench of justices Aravind Kumar and NV Anjaria, while the May 18 judgment was delivered by a bench of justices BV Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan. The bench headed by Justice Kumar responded to criticism of its own order and, in view of the perceived conflict, referred the matter to a larger bench. This order was passed while considering bail pleas for two other accused – Tasleem Ahmed and Abdul Khalid Saifi – in the 2020 Delhi riots case. The trial in the Delhi riots case involves 18 accused, and while Khalid and Imam remain in jail, other accused, including Gulfisha Fatima, Meeran Haider, Shifa Ur Rehman, Mohammad Saleem Khan and Shadab Ahmed, were granted bail by the same order of January 5. The Delhi police have invoked the UAPA and other provisions of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) against the accused. Out of the 18, only five, including the present petitioners, are in jail. The riots followed a protest against the Citizenship Amendment Act on February 24, 2020, that coincided with the visit of the US President. The police alleged this was deliberately timed to garner international attention. Khalid was arrested by the Delhi police on September 13, 2020, and has since been languishing in prison. Imam, on the other hand, was arrested in January 2020 in a separate hate speech case in Bihar and was formally arrested in the Delhi riots case on August 25, 2020.

The Centre on Thursday defended the proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions above ₹ 2,000, telling the Supreme Court that merchants were never assured that UPI payments would remain free indefinitely. In a counter-affidavit filed before the Supreme Court on November 4, the Union government said the revised MDR framework had been under consideration well before its introduction and was finalised after consulting stakeholders.
news.full_article_text: Merchants were never assured of zero MDR on UPI indefinitely: Govt to Supreme Court The Centre said person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions of up to ₹ 2,000 would be exempt from Merchant Discount Rate (MDR). The Centre on Thursday defended the proposed Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions above ₹ 2,000, telling the Supreme Court that merchants were never assured that UPI payments would remain free indefinitely. In a counter-affidavit filed before the Supreme Court on November 4, the Union government said the revised MDR framework had been under consideration well before its introduction and was finalised after consulting stakeholders. “Further, no specific assurance of a continuing zero-MDR regime was given to merchants, and the subsidy provided by the State was discretionary rather than obligatory,” the Centre said. The government was responding to a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by lawyer Anjan Datta, challenging the revised MDR framework. It defended the proposed charges against allegations that they violate the fundamental rights to equality and to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business under Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, respectively. Why the Centre says the ₹ 2,000 threshold is justified Defending the classification of transactions based on their value, payment mode and merchant category, the Centre said the framework meets the constitutional test of “intelligible differentia” under Article 14 and has a “rational nexus” with the objectives of financial inclusion, affordability and the long-term sustainability of the digital payments ecosystem. It said the ₹ 2,000 threshold was introduced to protect ordinary retail transactions and small merchants, while allowing higher-value transactions involving merchants considered better placed to bear a modest charge to attract MDR. The government also defended the differential treatment of UPI and RuPay debit cards, arguing that the two payment systems operate through distinct technological architectures, commercial arrangements and cost structures. It said the continued zero-MDR regime for RuPay advances the policy objective of promoting a domestic card network. Centre says MDR does not violate merchants' rights The Centre further argued that the revised framework does not impose an unreasonable restriction on merchants' right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g). It said the Constitution does not guarantee that commercial infrastructure must remain free of cost and that a charge which reduces a merchant's profit margin does not, by itself, amount to a violation of fundamental rights. The government also pointed out that merchants cannot pass on MDR charges to consumers. Addressing the allegation that the charges amount to an unauthorised levy, the Centre said MDR is neither a tax nor a fee imposed by the government. Instead, it described MDR as a “commercial payment deducted from a merchant's settlement under its arrangement with the acquiring bank”. The government said its role was limited to determining which electronic payment modes would remain exempt from charges under Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Commercial arrangements for transactions outside the exemption, including the determination of MDR, fall within the domain of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which operates UPI under authorisation from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). According to the Centre, NPCI determines the applicable charges and their distribution among participants in the payment ecosystem. Since the government neither fixes nor collects MDR, Article 265 of the Constitution, which prohibits the levy or collection of taxes without the authority of law, does not apply in this case, the affidavit stated. Centre cites ₹ 8,730 crore in subsidies Defending the economic rationale behind the revised framework, the government said the zero-MDR regime did not eliminate the cost of processing digital payments but merely shifted the financial burden to the government and other participants in the payment ecosystem. The Centre said it had disbursed ₹ 8,730 crore in incentives to acquiring banks between 2021-22 and 2024-25 to support zero-MDR transactions. However, citing reports of Parliamentary Standing Committees, it argued that these subsidies covered only a fraction of the estimated annual operating costs of the UPI ecosystem, which it placed at around ₹ 20,700 crore. The government said a “sustainable funding model” was necessary to support investments in cybersecurity, fraud prevention, dispute resolution, technological development and the expansion of digital payment infrastructure. Most UPI transactions to remain unaffected The Centre maintained that the revised framework would leave the overwhelming majority of UPI transactions unaffected. It said person-to-person (P2P) transactions would continue to remain exempt irrespective of their value. Person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions of up to ₹ 2,000 would also attract zero MDR. Additionally, transactions involving small merchants receiving up to ₹ 1 lakh a month through UPI QR codes would remain exempt from the proposed charges. The government also defended the legislative route adopted to introduce the revised framework. It argued that the amendment to Section 10A was validly passed as part of a Money Bill, as it had a direct bearing on government expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, given the subsidies previously provided to sustain zero-MDR transactions. What the UPI MDR case is before the Supreme Court In September 2026, while hearing the PIL filed by Anjan Datta challenging the revised MDR framework, the Supreme Court declined to stay its implementation. It issued notices to the Union government and NPCI, seeking their responses. The revised MDR framework was initially scheduled to come into effect on October 15, 2026. NPCI subsequently deferred its implementation. On November 3, NPCI also filed its counter-affidavit before the Supreme Court, defending the proposed charges. NPCI argued that MDR would apply to only a small fraction of P2M transactions, with around 96% of such transactions remaining unaffected under the revised framework. news.full_article_text: India successfully test-fires indigenously developed quasi-ballistic missile Pralay | Watch Pralay, developed by the DRDO, is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg. India on Thursday successfully test-fired quasi-ballistic missile Pralay from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the coast of Odisha. The missile, developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ), is capable of carrying conventional warheads, the defence ministry said in a statement. Pralay is a short-range surface-to-surface missile with a payload capacity of 500-1,000 kg. "With this successful test, the induction of the system has become imminent," the ministry said. Defence minister Rajnath Singh also complimented DRDO, Defence Forces and industry partners on the successful flight-test and said the missile equipped with advanced technologies will further enhance the technological capabilities and operational preparedness of the military against emerging threats. “The test was conducted as part of user evaluation trials and successfully met all the stipulated objectives, as validated by data captured through various range instruments. This successful trial marks another significant milestone in strengthening India’s indigenous defence capabilities,” Singh wrote in a post on X. The defence ministry said that all the test objectives were fully met as confirmed by the test data captured by various range instruments deployed by Integrated Test Range, Chandipur. Research Centre Imarat, Hyderabad, along with other DRDO laboratories, indigenously developed the missile, it said. Bharat Dynamics Limited, one of the development-cum-production-partners, has produced the system. The flight-test was conducted in the presence of senior officials from DRDO, representatives from the industry and the defence forces, as part of user evaluation trials, the ministry said in a statement. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR HT News Desk Follow the latest breaking news, major developments and agenda-setting stories from India and around the world with the newsdesk at Hindustan Times. news.headline: Former Supreme Court Justice Rajesh Bindal Appointed NCLAT Chairperson
news.story_lead: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rajesh Bindal has been appointed as the Chairperson of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT). His appointment fills the regular vacancy created after Justice Ashok Bhushan completed his term in July 2026. The appointment comes against the backdrop of recent observations by the Supreme Court concerning executive influence over tribunal administration.
news.full_article_text:
### Leadership Appointment at NCLAT
Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rajesh Bindal has been appointed as the Chairperson of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT). Justice Bindal retired from the apex court on April 15, 2026, after serving as a judge for over three years. Prior to his elevation to the Supreme Court in February 2023, he served as the Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court.

### Succession and Interim Arrangements
The post of NCLAT chairperson had remained without a permanent incumbent since former Supreme Court judge Justice Ashok Bhushan concluded his tenure on July 4, 2026. Following Justice Bhushan's retirement, Justice Yogesh Khanna, a judicial member of NCLAT, was appointed as the officiating chairperson starting July 5, 2026. The Central Government later extended Justice Khanna's officiating tenure in October 2026.

### Supreme Court Observations on Tribunal Autonomy
The appointment coincides with critical remarks made by the Supreme Court regarding administrative oversight of quasi-judicial bodies. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V Mohana expressed concern over the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' degree of control over the NCLT and NCLAT while hearing a petition filed by contractual employees.

CJI Surya Kant remarked that institutional autonomy was being compromised by executive control and emphasized that complete appointment autonomy should rest with tribunal leadership. As a measure to reform recruitment, the Supreme Court suggested deputation followed by phased regular recruitment through independent bodies such as the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) or the Staff Selection Commission (SSC).

### उत्तराधिकार और कार्यवाहक व्यवस्था
पूर्व सुप्रीम कोर्ट जज जस्टिस अशोक भूषण द्वारा 4 जुलाई 2026 को अपना कार्यकाल पूरा करने के बाद से NCLAT अध्यक्ष का पद स्थायी रूप से रिक्त था। जस्टिस भूषण की सेवानिवृत्ति के बाद, NCLAT के न्यायिक सदस्य जस्टिस योगेश खन्ना ने 5 जुलाई 2026 से कार्यवाहक अध्यक्ष का पद संभाला। केंद्र सरकार ने बाद में अक्टूबर 2026 में उनके कार्यवाहक कार्यकाल को बढ़ा दिया था।

### न्यायाधिकरण स्वायत्तता पर सुप्रीम कोर्ट की टिप्पणियाँ
यह नियुक्ति अर्ध-न्यायिक निकायों के प्रशासनिक नियंत्रण पर सुप्रीम कोर्ट द्वारा की गई गंभीर टिप्पणियों के साथ हुई है। भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश सूर्यकांत, जस्टिस जॉयमाल्या बागची और जस्टिस वी मोहना की पीठ ने संविदा कर्मचारियों द्वारा दायर याचिका पर सुनवाई के दौरान NCLT और NCLAT पर कॉर्पोरेट मामलों के मंत्रालय के नियंत्रण पर चिंता व्यक्त की।

सीजेआई सूर्यकांत ने टिप्पणी की कि कार्यकारी नियंत्रण से संस्थागत स्वायत्तता प्रभावित हो रही है और कर्मचारियों की नियुक्ति पर पूर्ण स्वायत्तता न्यायाधिकरण नेतृत्व के पास होनी चाहिए। सुधार के एक उपाय के रूप में, पीठ ने प्रतिनियुक्ति के बाद संघ लोक सेवा आयोग (UPSC) या कर्मचारी चयन आयोग (SSC) जैसे स्वतंत्र निकायों के माध्यम से नियमित भर्ती का सुझाव दिया।
